tagline: Israel's book of prayer and song: 150 poems of praise, lament, thanks, and wisdom, gathered into five books and prayed by God's people for three thousand years.
overview:
The Psalms are the prayer book of the Bible. Its 150 poems were written over many centuries by many hands, sung in the temple at Jerusalem, prayed in exile, and finally gathered into a single collection divided into five books. The Hebrew title is Tehillim, praises, though more of the psalms are laments than hymns. The English name comes through Greek and Latin from a word for songs sung to a stringed instrument. Here Israel speaks to God, and about God, in every condition a human life can reach: joy and terror, gratitude and guilt, confidence and the feeling of being abandoned.

The collection opens with two gateway psalms. Psalm 1 blesses the person who delights in God's instruction; Psalm 2 announces the king God has installed on Zion. Instruction and kingship, the life of the faithful individual and the fate of the anointed king, run through everything that follows. The five books move, very broadly, from the laments of David's reign, through the collapse of the Davidic monarchy mourned in Psalm 89, to the declaration that the LORD reigns whatever happens to Israel's kings, and on to a final crescendo in which every psalm from 146 to 150 begins and ends with Hallelujah, praise the LORD.

The book matters because it teaches people how to pray. Other parts of the Bible are God's word to his people; the Psalms are also his people's words to him, which he has taken into Scripture. They give permission to complain, to plead, to question, and to rage, and they keep bending those cries back toward trust and praise. Jews and Christians have prayed them daily for millennia, Jesus prayed them on the cross, and the New Testament quotes them as often as any Old Testament book.
author:
The Psalms have many authors, and the book itself says so. About half the psalms carry a heading (a superscription) naming a person. In the traditional Hebrew text, seventy-three are linked with David, twelve with Asaph (a Levite musician of David's time according to Chronicles), eleven or so with the sons of Korah (a guild of Levitical singers), two with Solomon, and one each with Moses, Heman, and Ethan. About a third have no heading at all. The Greek translation made before Jesus' time (the Septuagint) assigns still more psalms to David.

How to read these headings is debated. The Hebrew phrase usually translated of David can mean written by David, but it can also mean for David, belonging to a Davidic collection, or in the style of David. Many conservative scholars take the headings as reliable ancient tradition identifying the authors, pointing to David's reputation as a musician and poet in Samuel and Chronicles and to the New Testament's references to David as a psalmist (for example Acts 4:25). Many critical scholars regard the headings as later additions made by the editors of the collection, useful evidence of how the psalms were read but not proof of authorship. A middle view holds that the headings are old and often right, while recognizing that some mark a collection or a dedication rather than a writer. What no one disputes is that the Psalter gathers the voices of kings, Levites, and ordinary worshipers across many generations.
date:
The individual psalms span a long period, and the final collection came together at the end of it. Psalm 90 is attributed to Moses. Many psalms, especially in Books 1 and 2, are linked to David, who reigned around 1010 to 970 BC. Others clearly come from much later: Psalm 137 remembers sitting by the rivers of Babylon after Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC, and Psalm 126 celebrates the return from exile. Some scholars date a large share of the psalms to the time of the monarchy and its temple worship; others think many were composed or reshaped during or after the exile.

The gathering of the five books into their present form is usually placed in the Persian period (after 539 BC) or somewhat later, with the collection substantially complete by the second century BC. The Dead Sea Scrolls, copied between roughly the third century BC and the first century AD, include many psalms manuscripts, and some of them arrange the later psalms in a different order and add other compositions, which suggests that the last part of the collection was still settling in some circles around that time. The Septuagint numbers the psalms differently from the Hebrew for much of the book (it joins Psalms 9 and 10, for instance), which is why older Catholic and Orthodox Bibles sometimes number them one lower.
setting:
The psalms belong to the worship of ancient Israel, centered from Solomon's time on the temple in Jerusalem, on Mount Zion. Chronicles describes David organizing Levitical singers and musicians, and many headings contain musical or liturgical instructions whose meaning has been partly lost: the words for the choirmaster, names of tunes, instruments, and the frequent term Selah. Psalms were sung at the great pilgrimage festivals (the Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, were probably sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem), at the enthronement and weddings of kings, in times of national disaster, and in private distress.

The wider world presses in everywhere. Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon rise and fall in the background, enemy nations rage, and the psalms borrow and transform images common across the ancient Near East: the god who rides the storm, the chaos waters, the divine mountain, the king as the god's son. Canaanite poetry from Ugarit (on the Syrian coast, from before 1200 BC) shows striking parallels in style and imagery, and the psalms repeatedly take that language and give it to the LORD alone. After the temple fell in 586 BC, the psalms became the prayers of a scattered people, and in the synagogues that grew up later they became a large part of Jewish daily prayer.
purpose: The Psalter was gathered to be prayed and sung, first by Israel in the temple and later by Jews and Christians everywhere. It gives words to worshipers who have none of their own, and it shapes them over time: a person who prays the Psalms regularly learns to bring everything to God, to praise him for who he is, to confess sin honestly, to protest suffering without letting go of him, and to hope in his reign. The editors who arranged the five books also meant the whole to be read and meditated on as instruction, which is why it opens with Psalm 1's blessing on the one who meditates on God's law day and night. The arrangement answers a crisis. By the end of Book 3 the Davidic kingdom has fallen, and the later books teach Israel that the LORD is still king, that his promises to David still stand, and that praise, not despair, is the last word.
story: The Psalms don't narrate the story of Israel, but they sit inside every part of it. They look back to creation, to the exodus and the wilderness (Psalms 78, 105, 106), and to God's covenant with David (Psalms 89, 132). They sing through the reigns of the kings, the destruction of Jerusalem, the exile in Babylon, and the return. In the Christian Old Testament they stand among the books of poetry and wisdom, after Job and before Proverbs; in the Hebrew Bible they open the third division, the Writings, and Jesus can use the Psalms as a name for that whole section (Luke 24:44). The book carries forward the promise of a king from David's line, deepens the longing for God's reign over all nations, and teaches the prayer that the Gospels will place on Jesus' own lips.
christ:
The New Testament reads the Psalms as one of the clearest witnesses to Christ. Jesus himself said that everything written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). Some psalms are royal psalms about the anointed king from David's line, and the New Testament hears in them the true Son of David: Psalm 2 at Jesus' baptism and resurrection (Acts 13:33), Psalm 110 as the verse most quoted about his exaltation to God's right hand. Other psalms are the prayers of the suffering righteous, and the Gospels show Jesus praying them in his passion: he cries the opening of Psalm 22 from the cross, and Luke records his last words from Psalm 31.

This reading works at more than one level. Some texts the New Testament treats as direct prophecy of the Messiah; many others it treats as patterns that David's line and Israel's righteous sufferers could only partly fill, and that Jesus fills completely. Christians since the early church have prayed the Psalms both as their own prayers and as the prayers of Christ, the one who shares their suffering and leads their praise.
reading:
The Psalms are poetry, and they read best slowly and aloud. Hebrew poetry works mainly by parallelism: a second line echoes, sharpens, contrasts, or completes the first (the pattern was described systematically by Robert Lowth in the eighteenth century). Watch how the second line moves the thought forward rather than merely repeating it. Notice the genre of each psalm. Hermann Gunkel, in the early twentieth century, sorted the psalms into types that most scholars still use: hymns of praise, individual and communal laments, songs of thanksgiving, royal psalms, and wisdom psalms, with others such as songs of trust and songs of Zion. Laments usually move from complaint to petition to trust or praise, and that turn is often the heart of the psalm.

Two common misreadings are worth avoiding. The first is to treat the Psalms as a collection of comforting verses cut loose from their context; many of the best-known lines sit inside anguished prayers. The second is to be embarrassed by the laments and the curses on enemies. These are honest prayers that hand vengeance over to God rather than taking it, and they are part of what makes the book trustworthy. Reading a psalm in light of its neighbors and its place in the five books often reveals more than reading it alone.

structure.title: The gateway
structure.summary: Two untitled psalms introduce the whole book: the blessed life of the one who meditates on God's instruction, and the reign of the king God has installed on Zion.

structure.title: Book 1: David's prayers
structure.summary: Almost all attributed to David, many of them laments from danger and distress, with songs of trust and praise such as Psalms 8, 19, and 23. It closes with a doxology at 41:13.

structure.title: Book 2: Korah, David, and the king
structure.summary: Psalms of the sons of Korah and of David, which prefer the general word God to the name LORD. It ends with a prayer for the king (Psalm 72) and the note that the prayers of David son of Jesse are ended.

structure.title: Book 3: The crisis
structure.summary: Mostly psalms of Asaph and Korah, full of communal lament over the ruin of the sanctuary and the nation. It ends with Psalm 89, which asks how God's covenant with David can stand when the crown lies in the dust.

structure.title: Book 4: The LORD reigns
structure.summary: Opening with a prayer of Moses, this book answers the crisis by looking back past the monarchy to God as Israel's eternal dwelling place, and by proclaiming that the LORD is king (Psalms 93 and 95 to 99).

structure.title: Book 5: Return and thanksgiving
structure.summary: Psalms of thanksgiving for rescue, the great meditation on God's word in Psalm 119, the Songs of Ascents for pilgrims, and a final group of Davidic psalms, with Psalm 110's royal priest-king at its center.

structure.title: The final Hallelujah
structure.summary: Five psalms that each begin and end with praise the LORD, closing the book with everything that has breath praising God.

themes.title: The LORD is king
themes.body: Beneath every lament and every hymn lies the conviction that the LORD reigns over creation, over the nations, and over Israel. The king God installs on Zion rules on his behalf, but when that human kingship fails, the Psalms insist that God's own reign has not. This theme ties the collection together and points forward to the kingdom Jesus announced.

themes.title: Lament and honest prayer
themes.body: The largest group of psalms are laments. They complain to God about enemies, sickness, guilt, and God's own apparent absence, and they do so inside the covenant rather than against it. Most turn, sometimes abruptly, toward trust. A few, like Psalm 88, never do. Their presence in Scripture shows that protest can be a form of faith.

themes.title: Praise and thanksgiving
themes.body: Praise in the Psalms is response: to God's work in creation, to his rescue of Israel, and to his help in a particular crisis. Thanksgiving psalms often retell the distress and the deliverance before the congregation, so that one person's rescue becomes the whole community's reason to worship.

themes.title: The two ways
themes.body: Beginning with Psalm 1, the collection contrasts the righteous and the wicked, the way that God watches over and the way that perishes. The wisdom psalms (such as 1, 37, 49, 73, and 112) wrestle openly with the fact that the wicked often prosper, and they locate the answer in God's judgment and presence rather than in quick rewards.

themes.title: God's instruction
themes.body: The Psalter opens by blessing the person who delights in the law (torah, meaning instruction) of the LORD, and it returns to the theme in Psalms 19 and 119. The whole book is offered as instruction to be meditated on, so that praying and learning belong together.
